January 23
Epiphany 3C — The Third Sunday of Epiphany 
Colors: green
Lk 4:14-21
1 Cor 12:12-27
Neh 8:1-12
Psalm 113


To the Saints at Vanadium Woods,
January 23, 2022
Grace and peace from our Lord Jesus Christ, the son of our Father in Heaven, the builder of his Church.


The lectionary editors, the people who make the reading selections, catch a lot of flak from me over how often I think they didn't do a good job - Like today's Gospel reading (Luke 4:14-21) that ends halfway through the story. And guess what? The story concludes in next week's Gospel reading. The obvious answer to this conundrum is to not talk about the Gospel. Sadly, I don't like the obvious answer. Even so, every time I started working out what needed to be said, I wound up jumping to the conclusion, which is in next week's Gospel. Through sheer cussed force of will I would start over saying to myself, "What does today's and only today's Gospel tell us?"


What comes immediately before today's reading is the story of Jesus' Temptation in the Desert. It is sort of easy to jump over the first handful of verses where Jesus went about the region and taught in the synagogues, being "glorified by all." 


Luke does not give us any details.


By the time Jesus gets to his hometown of Nazareth he has developed a good reputation. We can imagine the folks who regularly attended synagogue worship in Nazareth were anxious to hear him. Jesus reads from the Prophet Isaiah, the beginning of the 61st chapter


“The Spirit of the Lord is upon me,
    because he has anointed me
    to proclaim good news to the poor.
    He has sent me to proclaim liberty to the captives
    and recovering of sight to the blind
    to set at liberty those who are oppressed,
    to proclaim the year of the Lord’s favor.”


When he finishes, Jesus sits down. We would not find this unusual because nowadays when someone finishes reading a passage, they sit down. They sit down and don't say another word as they wait for the preacher to stand up and say something. Back in the Bad'ol Days, the preacher sat down while everyone else stood to listen. I am afraid nowadays, if folks stood to hear the sermon, they might slowly start shuffling towards the back door.


But Jesus sat down because he had something to say about the passage from Isaiah. In that time, it was held by the faithful that Isaiah was looking towards sometime in the future when the promised Messiah would come. It must have come as a shock to hear Jesus say, "Today this Scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing."


I can't help but imagine more than one person thought to themselves, "I wonder who he is talking about?" followed quickly by, "Waaaait a minute..." It becomes clear to even the dullest of listeners that Jesus is talk about himself - how that works out will have to wait till next week, but what we want to ask this week is, "What does Jesus have to say about himself?" 


Jesus is being pretty clear that he, himself, is the Messiah appointed by God. This is a tall claim and would be a bit hard to swallow back then. Furthermore, it is Jesus’ intention to bring blessings to those who have not been blessed: the poor, the captives, the blind, and liberty to the oppressed.


At this point I was sorely tempted to go on about the dangers of wealth and then had a good think about you all and thought, "complete waste of everyone's time." Besides, that's not what Jesus is talking about here. He talks about the dangers of money in other places. What Jesus talks about here is the blessings coming to those who have experienced real and serious hardships.


As I thought about this group in general, it occurred to me these are the people who make church folks uncomfortable when they come to church. I had to stop a moment and have a think about who makes me uncomfortable when they come to church, besides Bishops, I mean. The real truth in our age where Jesus has been revealed to us as the Son of God and Redeemer, is the people who make us uncomfortable in church are the very ones we need to have with us. 


I always think of my dear, sweet Aunt Mary, who said to me she didn't go to church because it was filled with hypocrites. You've probably heard or felt similar. But the truth is, it is those very hypocrites who need to be welcomed with open arms.


One of the sad things about Church history is the way we've divided ourselves from each other, and it's all our own fault. The Church in Corinth that St. Paul was always writing to had this sort of problem. It was filled with every variety of Christian you could imagine, rich - poor, slave - free, male - female, Jews and Greeks, those who spoke in tongues and those who did not, and on and on. What St. Paul makes abundantly clear to the Corinthians is that in spite of their differences, they were all in desperate need of each other.


One of the saddest lines from 1 Corinthians we read today is, "If the foot should say, “Because I am not a hand, I do not belong to the body,” that would not make it any less a part of the body"  *1 Corinthians 12:15* How is it that the foot should not feel like it belongs to the body? I don't know about you, but I like my feet right where they are, even if I don't want to show them off in public. The point for the Church being, that those who do not feel like they belong should, by all means, be made welcome.


Because of the way us humans are, making some people welcome is not an easy task. In my own darker moments, I have thought, "Boy howdy, if THAT person ever showed up here they would NOT get communion." I confess this as a sin and not worthy of a member of Christ's own Church. But then, I am not worthy of Christ's own Church and there are precious few that are. It is the ones who are in need of redemption who need to be here, and I am one of them.


I wish I could, with a straight face, say to you, "Be more like me," to me, that is a truly frightening thought. Our goal is to be more like Christ. That, too, is a frightening thought, but for a different reason. The standard for Christ-like behavior is so high it is not within our grasp. That is, it is not within our grasp without the power of the Holy Spirit, which is something we have access to. So, it really is within our grasp but requires practice.


The take home is, the ones who require the most Christ-like behavior from us are the very ones we need, yes need, to have with us.


The peace of God, which passes all understanding, keep your hearts and minds in the knowledge and love of God, and of His Son Jesus Christ our Lord; and the blessing of God Almighty, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, be among you, and remain with you always. 
paul+
